    Track 2 · Hands-on · Lesson 7

    Evaluate by hand: run the gold set, compute the metric

    After this lesson you can load your fine-tuned adapter, generate predictions on the gold set, compute a metric, and compare the fine-tuned model against the base baseline to prove the lift.

    Level: intermediate Read time: ~10 min Prerequisites: Run it: read the logs, the loss, the checkpoints Updated: 13 Nov 2026

    Training produced an adapter. Now we answer the only question that matters: is it better than the base model on our task? We'll load the adapter, run it over the gold set, compute accuracy, and — crucially — compare to the untuned baseline.

    Load the base + adapter

    LoRA keeps the base frozen, so inference is "base model + adapter." PeftModel.from_pretrained attaches your trained adapter to a fresh base:

    import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
from peft import PeftModel

model_id = "HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-135M-Instruct"
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
use_bf16 = torch.cuda.is_available() and torch.cuda.is_bf16_supported(including_emulation=False)
use_fp16 = torch.cuda.is_available() and not use_bf16
dtype = torch.bfloat16 if use_bf16 else (torch.float16 if use_fp16 else torch.float32)   # Lesson 2.1

tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("sft-out/adapter")
base = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, dtype=dtype).to(device)
tuned = PeftModel.from_pretrained(base, "sft-out/adapter").eval()

    PEFT modifies the model you pass in

    PeftModel.from_pretrained(base, …) injects the LoRA layers into base in place. After that line, base is the tuned model: scoring it gives the tuned accuracy, and the lift always reads 0. To get the real baseline, score the base before attaching the adapter, or switch the adapter off with tuned.disable_adapter(), as below.

    A prediction helper

    We use greedy decoding (do_sample=False) so results repeat run to run on the same hardware and batch size (GPU kernels and padding can still flip a near-tie elsewhere) — exactly what Track 1 recommended for evaluation. The completion is short (a label), so a handful of new tokens is enough.

    @torch.no_grad()
def predict(model, prompt):
    msgs = [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]
    text = tok.apply_chat_template(msgs, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True)
    ids = tok(text, return_tensors="pt").to(model.device)
    out = model.generate(**ids, max_new_tokens=8, do_sample=False,
                         pad_token_id=tok.pad_token_id)
    return tok.decode(out[0][ids["input_ids"].shape[1]:], skip_special_tokens=True).strip().lower()

    Score the gold set

    import json
with open("gold.jsonl") as f:                # saved in Lesson 2.3: 200 rows, never trained on
    gold = [json.loads(line) for line in f]   # each row: {"prompt": ..., "label": "positive" | "negative"}

def accuracy(model):
    hits = sum(predict(model, ex["prompt"]).startswith(ex["label"]) for ex in gold)
    return hits / len(gold)

with tuned.disable_adapter():               # the base, with the adapter switched off
    base_acc = accuracy(tuned)
tuned_acc = accuracy(tuned)                 # adapter back on
print("base  accuracy:", base_acc)          # the baseline
print("tuned accuracy:", tuned_acc)         # after fine-tuning
print("lift:", tuned_acc - base_acc)
# one CPU run (Lesson 2.3's 200 gold rows): base 0.015, tuned 0.85, lift 0.835

    Two things to keep in mind when you read these numbers. First, startswith is a strict format check: the untuned model answers in a full sentence (Lesson 2.2), which scores as wrong even when the sentiment in it is right, so part of any lift here is the model learning the output format. In the run above the base scored 0.015 because it answers in sentences. A lenient check that accepts the label anywhere in the answer scores the same base at 0.505, about chance on this balanced set: the base says "negative" on most rows, so 0.505 is roughly the share of negative gold rows (0.51). So more than half of the 0.835 lift, about 0.49, is the model learning to answer with a bare label, and the rest, about 0.35, is real sentiment skill. Second, the gold set must be big enough to mean something: with two rows, accuracy can only be 0%, 50% or 100%, and even at Lesson 2.3's 200 rows a 90% score has a 95% interval of roughly ±4 points.

    Small test sets: is the difference real?

    Score both models on the same rows and look at the change row by row (a paired comparison), not just at the two headline numbers. On a small test set one answer moves the score a lot: one row in 20 is 5 points, one in 50 is 2.

    BrewSLM pairs the rows, counts how many got better, worse or stayed the same, and puts a 95% confidence interval (a paired t-interval) around the mean change. If the interval includes zero, the change is within noise: the data cannot tell a gain from a loss. Under 5 paired rows it gives no verdict.

    Worked example: 50 test rows
    Base model22 right (44%)
    Fine-tuned26 right (52%): +8 points
    Row by row6 better, 2 worse, 42 the same
    95% interval−3 to +19 points: within noise
    Visible gapabout 16 points at this size; about 500 rows to see a 5-point change

    Habits that keep a small test honest:

    • Compare like with like: same rows, same answer key, same scoring and decoding settings. BrewSLM's Compare gives no verdict when the answer key, judge or scoring differ.
    • Practice, then final: iterate against the practice answer key and score the final one rarely. A set you consult on every decision ends up fitted to your choices.
    • Small slices are noise: a per-class or per-entity score on a handful of rows swings on one row. Show the row count next to it.
    • Seeds: two or three training seeds show how much runs vary; with that few the interval is wide, so read the spread as a rough sign of the noise, not as a test.

    Further reading: Evan Miller, "Adding Error Bars to Evals" (arXiv 2411.00640).

    Always report the lift

    A single accuracy number means little. The difference between the tuned model and the base — the lift — is what your fine-tune actually bought. If tuned ≈ base, fine-tuning didn't help; revisit the data (Track 1) before anything else.

    Read the failures, not just the score

    Honest evaluation (Track 1) means looking at what the model gets wrong, not just the headline number. Print the misses:

    for ex in gold:
    pred = predict(tuned, ex["prompt"])
    if not pred.startswith(ex["label"]):
        print(f"WRONG  pred={pred!r}  gold={ex['label']!r}  :: {ex['prompt']}")

    Those misses are your to-do list: they tell you which kinds of examples to add or fix in the training data for the next iteration. That data-centric loop is the heart of getting good. Once you're satisfied with the lift, the last step is packaging the model for use — merging the adapter and shipping an artifact.

    Recap

    • Score the base and the tuned model on the same gold set with greedy decoding, and report the difference: the lift.
    • PeftModel.from_pretrained changes the base you pass in; take the baseline inside with tuned.disable_adapter():.
    • startswith also checks the format, so read the misses: they are the to-do list for your next data pass.

    Try it (5 minutes)

    Score the base twice: once with the lesson's startswith check and once with a lenient check that only asks whether the right label appears anywhere in the answer (ex["label"] in pred). Before you run it, predict which number moves, and what the gap between the two numbers tells you.

    Show answer

    The lenient score is the one that moves. In our CPU run the base went from 0.015 with startswith to 0.505 with the lenient check: it answers "the sentiment is positive." and the like, which startswith marks wrong. 0.505 is about chance on this balanced gold set, so the base's real sentiment skill is close to nil and the tuned model's 0.85 is about 0.35 of real gain plus about 0.49 of format. Report both numbers, format compliance and label accuracy, so a reader can tell which kind of lift you got.

    Key terms

    PeftModel.from_pretrained
    Attaches a trained LoRA adapter onto a fresh base model for inference.
    greedy decoding
    do_sample=False — deterministic generation, used for reproducible evaluation.
    accuracy
    Fraction of gold examples predicted correctly (a classification metric).
    baseline comparison
    Scoring the untuned base on the same gold set to measure the fine-tune's lift.
    failure analysis
    Reading the wrong predictions to decide what data to fix next.
